analysis.one_liner: Caps U.S. prescription drug prices at 6% above average prices in five other industrialized countries.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote and died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the President to set rules ensuring no drug sold to U.S. consumers costs more than 6% above its average retail price in the five most industrialized free-market countries other than the United States. It would give federal officers subpoena power to examine drug makers' records, allow fines of up to 200% of unlawful sales, and let consumers sue for damages and attorneys' fees. The bill was referred to two House committees and never moved further.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers who pay for prescription drugs, including seniors and uninsured patients who face the highest drug prices in the world; the bill also gives private citizens a right to sue over overcharged sales and recover fees.

how_it_helps.text: Caps what any U.S. consumer can be charged for a drug at 6% above the average retail price in the five most industrialized free-market countries other than the United States.

Authorizes the Attorney General to seek injunctions and restitution against drug companies that sell above the cap, and allows criminal fines and civil penalties of up to 200% of the unlawful sale or unjust enrichment.
Creates a private right of action letting overcharged consumers recover actual damages, punitive damages, and attorneys' fees, including through class actions.
Gives the enforcing officer power to examine drug makers' books and records and summon testimony to verify compliance with the price limits.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, which currently charge far more in the United States than in other wealthy countries and would lose that pricing premium; some of the lost revenue could come at the expense of future research spending.

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves the key definition, the choice of comparison countries, and all implementing rules to the discretion of the President, so the actual strength of the price cap would depend entirely on whoever holds the office.

Tighter price limits could reduce the revenue pharmaceutical companies reinvest in developing new drugs, a cost the bill's own findings acknowledge by stating that producers must still be 'appropriately compensated'.
Building a new federal enforcement system — including record inspections, summons, agency hearings, and litigation — would require substantial appropriations for fiscal years 2001 through 2003.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Lower drug prices would be a real, immediate gain for the many Americans who pay the highest prices in the world for medicines. The bill's design is crude, though: it delegates nearly everything to presidential discretion, and the trade-off with research investment is genuine. A more carefully built version might have targeted the same goal with clearer definitions and narrower enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to two House committees, and sent to a health subcommittee, and it sat there without ever getting a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Major Owens introduced the bill on June 27, 2000, near the end of the 106th Congress.
It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the House Judiciary Committee.
On July 19, 2000, the portion under Commerce's jurisdiction was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and no further action was taken.
The bill never reached a committee vote or a House floor vote, and the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers came out ahead: with the bill dead, they kept the freedom to charge U.S. consumers more than they charge in other wealthy countries, and U.S. patients continued paying among the highest drug prices in the world.

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five cosponsors, all Democrats.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no further action after referral; its health subcommittee received the bill on July 19, 2000, and no markup or vote ever followed.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats supported the bill in the record — one sponsor and five Democratic cosponsors — but no vote was ever taken, so no one is recorded opposing it.

industries.note: The bill would cap U.S. prices at roughly the average of five other industrialized countries, erasing the premium American patients currently pay — U.S. prices are typically far higher. It also exposes drug makers to fines of up to 200% of unlawful sales and consumer lawsuits.
Generics are generally already priced near international levels, so the cap would bind them rarely, if at all, while a cheaper U.S. drug market could expand the volume they sell.
